implementation_notes: JavaScript objects are plain data, so a test-support module exporting 'createCustomer(overrides = {})' replaces the classic mother class; default parameters and object spread ({...base, ...overrides}) give named canned objects and cheap variation without a framework, and node:test can assert on them directly. Return a fresh object per call - never a module-level constant - and clone nested objects, because spread is shallow.
pitfalls: A module-level fixture object handed out by reference is mutated by the first test that touches it; build a fresh object and rebuild nested objects too (spread copies references).
Spread overrides are shallow: passing address: {city: 'Rome'} replaces the whole address instead of merging, silently dropping street and zip.
Dates, Maps and class instances are not cloned by spread, so a factory returning a shared Date gives every test the same mutable instant.

variants.name: Declarative factories with fishery
variants.implementation_notes: fishery moves the same idea to declarative factories: Factory.define(({sequence}) => ({...})) with defaults, typed params and build({...}) overlays; associations and sequence give per-call uniqueness, and buildList covers collections. Prefer it once a suite has more than a handful of fixtures or needs per-call variation, and keep the plain factory functions for one-off canned examples.
pitfalls: Params are overlaid shallowly too: nested objects passed to build() replace the default subtree unless associations are used.
Sequence values depend on how many objects were built earlier in the process, so assertions on generated ids must not assume a start value.
Factories defined at module scope with mutable state (counters, caches) behave differently under test-file parallelism.
